thread.title: This mobile payment app takes aim at America’s highest-spending tourists - MarketWatch

author: Maria Lamagna
title: This mobile payment app takes aim at America’s highest-spending tourists - MarketWatch
text:
Published: Mar 21, 2018 12:55 p.m. ET Share 
Alipay is expanding in the U.S. — but not because it wants American users Fred Dufour/AFP/Getty Images Chinese shoppers buy 32% of luxury goods worldwide. 
By Reporter 
Chinese tourists will soon have an easier way of shopping in the U.S. 
Alipay announced this week it will be accepted by 35,000 additional merchants in the U.S. The Chinese mobile payment platform is an affiliate of mega-retailer Alibaba BABA, -1.83% and owned by the financial services company Ant Financial. 
Those new merchants are in addition to the 4 million U.S. merchant locations that Alipay and First Data announced in May 2017. The expansion of Alipay, which already has over 600 million users, is possible through a partnership with Atlanta-based First Data FDC, -1.69% which facilitates the payments through its point-of-sale platforms. 
The reason for the integration? “Alipay aims to simplify every aspect of Chinese tourists’ travel in North America, enabling them to use Alipay for everything from ride-hailing and purchasing luxury goods, to making reservations at hotels and restaurants,” the company said in a statement. 
Currently, Alipay only works when linked with Chinese bank accounts. It works without the use of a credit card, making payments possible directly between bank accounts and retailers. 
Alipay isn’t the only company making shopping in the U.S. easier for those used to shopping in China. The payments company ACI Worldwide ACIW, -0.35% on Wednesday announced a partnership with the Chinese company UnionPay International, which allows more UnionPay cards to be accepted at merchants worldwide. There are more than 7 billion UnionPay cards that have been issued worldwide. 
“If you’re a U.S. retailer, and you’re seeing the growth of Chinese tourism, there’s this opportunity to capture those tourist dollars coming into your store,” said Brendan Miller, a principal analyst at the research firm Forrester. 
Travel from China to the U.S. will likely only grow as more Chinese citizens increase their income, said Ryan Tuttle, a senior consumer finance analyst at the research firm Euromonitor International. They are a powerful economic force for U.S. retailers. Some 2.97 million Chinese tourists spent $33 billion in the U.S. in 2016 , up 9% from the previous year, according to a U.S. Commerce Department report. That’s more than any other nationality, the report found. 
What’s more, Chinese nationals bought 32% of all luxury goods worldwide in 2017 , according to the consulting firm Bain. Apparel, beauty and handbags make up the three biggest luxury categories consumers are buying worldwide, and shoes, jewelry and handbags are the three fastest-growing categories, it found. 
Making payments easier for Chinese tourists will likely be a priority for luxury brand retailers and duty-free shops at airports, as well as transportation services, Miller said. 
But Alipay probably won’t pick up too many new American users, even if Alipay could connect with U.S.-based bank accounts, Tuttle said. In the U.S., familiar mobile payment systems such as Apple Pay AAPL, -2.27% and Samsung Pay 005930, +0.27% still have relatively low adoption rates, so it’s “really unlikely” Alipay would start to take off among Americans, Tuttle said. 
“So much of whether a payment gets used is its ubiquity,” he said. “Nobody wants to be the one holding up the line at the store.” 
What’s more, American consumers might be less likely to trust a payment system so closely associated with an overseas company, at a time when there are growing concerns about access to data, he said. They already have shown some distrust of American companies like Amazon AMZN, -0.29% Facebook FB, +0.74% and Google GOOG, -0.62% having access to so much of their data. 
Facebook, in particular, is embroiled in a scandal involving the alleged data breach of 50 million accounts through a third party app. “With Facebook data news coming out this week, people are becoming more aware of who has their data,” Tuttle said. See also
